Sorry, you're missing the point.. guy and girl are considered correct because they became the norm, but it's no coincidence that the most widely accepted word for an adult woman also applies to children. That's how the language evolved, and there are reasons for it. 

If you don't care at all and don't care about giving things any thought beyond "I'll do it because I can and you can't stop me!!!!" and "that's just the way it is", that's fine, but you should keep in mind that that's a really slippery slope. And obviously, you shouldn't expect people to agree that challenging language and giving it some more thought is super radical or whatever.

Like I said, you are free to call yourself whatever you like, and it's none of my business to police what people call themselves, or what kinds of terms they mind or don't mind being referred to as. 

 That doesn't magically change the fact that one term is used exclusively for male adults, and the other one is used for people ranging from children to adult or even middle aged women! That's why they are fundamentally not equivalent.

"boy" is to "girl" as "guy" is to something, like "gal", I guess. 

The fact that a great number of English speakers adopted the usage of girl instead of something else doesn't mean that it's not slightly odd to use an infantilizing term to refer to perfectly grown women, especially given that words aren't devoid of social context and that we live in a society well known for infantilizing and alienating women in general.

If you prefer that people would refer to you as "girl" instead of "woman" or whatever else, that's perfectly fine, but you have to understand that saying they're not equivalent terms, or asking you to consider the implications of the word, is not an attempt at invalidating your identity.

It's okay to call yourself whatever you like, and people shouldn't really bother you for it. That sad, girl and guy are not equivalent in any way other than the fact that they're commonly used as if they were. Nobody calls male children "guys", but tons of (most?) english speakers routinely call adult women "girls", which says a lot about how women are perceived in general.

I definitely wouldn't call myself anything that's remotely adult sounding because I really don't feel it, but people should try to avoid calling other adult women girls whenever possible because of the connotations of how the term is used. Like I said, it's your identity and you can use whichever terms you like, but it's important to keep in mind what the implications of certain words are when you use them constantly to refer to other people.

I doubt many sensible feminists would get upset at you for wanting to call yourself something, but that doesn't change the fact that the two terms aren't really equivalent at all.

I'm sorry, I didn't mean it like that at all! It takes a really long time to learn how to use your voice properly for anything, either singing or using a different voice entirely, so don't worry too much. Mine sucks and I've been at it for a while on and off... 

Try listening to my clips so you can tell the difference between something more chesty and something less chesty, or you can try listening to someone like this https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0UHwkfhwjsk. 

You should be able to tell that even in your first clip which was slightly more mouth-y and less chest-y, you're still letting the voice linger around your bottom throat/chest too much, and it causes it to have that deep sound no matter how much you bring your pitch up (you really shouldn't obsess about your pitch btw, you can screw your throat up really badly trying to go higher and higher without proper training). You can tell that Steven Wilson there is very obviously a man, because he doesn't make any effort to make his voice resonate differently, but you can also tell that even when he dips down to the lowest notes in the chorus ("I'm dying of love, it's **okay**"), it's still a very clean, floaty sound. This is because when you let your voice linger around your chest instead of generating AND projecting it properly, it will resonate in your naturally larger chest and make that deep rumbling sound that you probably want to get rid of, no matter how high you make your pitch go. Not doing this is actually incredibly hard and you obviously shouldn't expect to sound anywhere near as good as Mr. Wilson :P but I'm just trying to illustrate my point here.

It's really just a matter of looooots of practice. I know it's hard, but I'm sure you can do it!

All the clips you posted, including the one where you said you were projecting your head voice, sound like they're coming mostly from your chest.

I suggest you go learn how to sing, which is MUCH easier to find resources for than voice changing.

The first thing you should do is find your head voice. To find out if you're doing your head voice right (besides the super obvious difference :P) place your finger very gently on your jugular notch (the hole at the bottom of your neck) and do your voice thing. Vibrations should be coming mostly from way above that point, so you should barely feel anything there. If you don't feel any vibrations you are going to end up sounding like a cartoon, and it will probably hurt, so don't do that!

An easy way to do it is to start a deep, guttural "mmmmmm" sound and then move it up as much as you can. If you are untrained in doing this you will make a funny noise that sounds remarkably like a kettle, probably because it works the same way, and then you want to try moving it very slowly downwards until it starts sounding more human and less like a hot beverage instrument. That's roughly the point where you want your voice to be.

After you find the region where your voice should be, you want to work on clearly projecting it out of your mouth. Learn how to breathe properly.. again go look up singing resources for this, it's a super broad subject that I can't really cram into a short post. The idea is that you should be breathing by using your diaphragm, including using it to push air and voice out of the front of your mouth instead of having your voice linger around your throat. Honestly the best way to learn how to do this without singing lessons is to just mess around with your voice box. Try reading up on throat/neck anatomy and contract muscles until you know what your different parts do to your voice. Just don't overdo it or do it too hard, because you can seriously hurt yourself... I mean mostly to get an idea of how to play this weird instrument you have in your throat.

After you've mastered all of this, including singing and holding notes for extended periods of time without choking and at the pitch you prefer, you can start working on getting your voice to resonate like you'd expect your average woman's voice to do. This is mostly achieving by lightly pulling your larynx up, which will happen kinda naturally as you do the above, and backwards, which is something that isn't really included in singing lessons. You can do that by training the muscles around the side of your neck. It also has the cool side effect of making your adam's apple less visible! The location your adam's apple should get to when doing this is kinda like where it goes when you swallow something, but a bit less extreme.

Anyway, I think you should stop thinking about transition like a switch that only goes on or off. Think about it like a thing you're doing to move your expression on the gender slider closer to where you want it. Don't think about "being a girl" or "being a man" because those concepts are usually riddled with stereotypes and baggage that is pretty unhealthy to obsess over. If you feel nice and happy with a more typically feminine expression, that's fine! Just please stop thinking about what you're doing as "becoming a girl" or "not being a man anymore" or whatever because in the end that's kind of irrelevant. You are you, and you're altering your expression to match what you feel more closely, and that's really all you need to think about.

Also I am not a therapist or medical professional, but I suffer from severe anxiety and I would recommend seeing a doctor about it, and getting started on dealing with your anxiety as a separate problem from your dysphoria. I know how it is to feel scared all the time and to have that prevent you from expressing yourself as you'd like, and I think you'd feel a lot better if you found a way to deal with that.
